title: Unequal Coherent Ergotropy at Equal Interferometric Visibility and Energy in Quantum-Controlled Interferometers
authors: Tonipe Anuradha, André H. A. Malavazi, Borhan Ahmadi, Lucas Pollyceno, Pedro R. Dieguez
abstract: The ergotropy, or unitarily extractable work, of a quantum system naturally splits into incoherent and coherent contributions, respectively set by population inversion and coherences in the energy eigenbasis. We show that this split makes the coherent ergotropy of a Mach--Zehnder qubit sensitive to path predictability that the output interference fringes do not reveal. We send the path qubit, prepared as a thermal quantum battery, through two quantum-controlled interferometers built from the same elements, a fixed beam splitter and a beam splitter coherently controlled to be present or absent, differing only in the order in which these two act. The two arrangements share identical visibility, stored energy, and incoherent ergotropy at every point in the parameter space. Yet, for work extracted from the output battery alone, placing the controlled beam splitter first never yields less coherent ergotropy, and at fixed visibility and interferometric phase the difference is governed by the path predictability that this ordering creates. The same expression reappears as a purity deficit on the beam-splitter controller, so the work advantage comes with a Landauer bound on the cost of locally resetting the controller that is never larger at the same temperature. We further examine the effects of decoherence on the battery and consider a relativistic realization in which a Wigner rotation correlates the particle's spin with its path. Tracing out the spin decoheres the battery and allows the two arrangements to exhibit different coherent ergotropies even in regimes where their non-relativistic counterparts coincide. These results show that interference visibility is not a complete measure of the coherence available as work.
summary: This paper analyzes quantum interferometers to show that the extractable work (coherent ergotropy) depends not just on the output interference pattern, but also on the sequence of quantum operations performed. By comparing two setups, the authors demonstrate that path predictability, which is hidden from visibility measurements, dictates the available work. This highlights that visibility is an incomplete measure of quantum coherence for work extraction.
main_problem: The study investigates whether the coherent ergotropy (unitarily extractable work) in quantum interferometers is sensitive to path predictability in ways that are invisible to standard measures like interference visibility.
main_result: The order of operations in the interferometer setup (QDCE vs. QCRE) can lead to different amounts of extractable coherent work, even when visibility and stored energy are identical.
method: The authors compare two quantum-controlled interferometer arrangements by calculating the coherent ergotropy for both, extending the analysis to relativistic regimes.
model_or_system: The system uses a two-level system (TLS) traversing a Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (MZI) whose beam-splitter control is governed by an auxiliary quantum degree of freedom, acting as a quantum battery.
key_observables: Coherent Ergotropy, Interference Visibility (V), Path Predictability (P), Which-Way Distinguishability (D), and the Landauer bound cost.

main_assumptions: The analysis assumes $\hbar=1$ and compares non-relativistic and relativistic limits where spin decoherence is introduced.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the two comparative setups: the Quantum Delayed-Choice Experiment (QDCE) and the Quantum-Controlled Reality Experiment (QCRE) using BS gates.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the theoretical predictions for ergotropy and related coherence measures between the QDCE and QCRE setups, first in the non-relativistic limit, and then extending the formalism to include relativistic spin correlations.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, measurable example showing that thermodynamic work extraction (ergotropy) is a more sensitive measure of quantum coherence than simple interference visibility, linking quantum measurement theory to thermodynamics.
